content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies LLMs’ performance in answering a composition of two questions vs. answering each question separately and how this performance gap (compositionality gap) evolves with scale. They find this gap does not shrink using vanilla in-context learning with scale, but decreases using more sophisticated methods of prompting LLMs, such as chain of thought or their proposed method called self-ask (similar to CoT with more structure). They also observe that as models get more confident in their answers to each single question it is more probable for the LM to compose two facts and answer the compositional question. 

Key contributions are:
* Studying the compositional gap using 1-hop and 2-hop questions
* Two new dataset, Compositional Celebrities (CC) and Bamboogle (125 examples) with 2-hop questions
* Self-ask prompting
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
The proposed method of using 2-hop questions as a way of evaluating the compositional abilities of large language models.

The automatically generated 2-hop QA Compositional Celebrities dataset with the constraint that the two facts/questions in each example, have been seen during pretraining separately with a high probability, but not together.

The proposed self-ask prompting method is more structured than Chain of Thought prompting which enables the authors to use it in combination with a search engine to boost the performance. 

### Weaknesses
The author's study of this compositional gap is limited to k-hop questions with k=2. Studying k>2 instances or other types of tasks (e.g. [Qui et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12253)) would shed more light on the compositional abilities of LLMs. 

The term “multi-hop” has been used a couple of times in the paper. It would be better to change them to 2-hop since that is the only setting experimented with.

Studying k>2 instances or other types of tasks could also be useful in evaluating the proposed prompting method (self-ask) with longer reasoning chains and decomposition of questions. I think a more thorough evaluation of this method is missing from the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written and mostly clear. Only a few comments:

* It would be nice to keep the colors the same in Figure 1 and 4.
* What is the reason for the self-ask method answering more compositional questions than separate 1-hop questions in Figure 4? It is mentioned that “This might be because elicitive prompts contain more information than direct ones”. This is a bit unclear. Could you elaborate?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies an important topic of compositional abilities of large language models in a clever way using k-hop QA datasets where k is limited to 2. The authors propose a prompting method, called self-ask, similar to Chain of Thought with more structure and versatility to improve compositional abilities of large language models. However, a more comprehensive evaluation of this method would be appreciated.

content.title: k-hop questions
content.comment:
Thanks for your review! We’re glad you liked our compositionality gap experiments, self-ask prompting, and the self-ask + search engine system. 

Your main suggestion was that we should consider compositional questions with more than 2-hops, and we agree that this would be a fantastic direction for future work. Given that we wanted an in depth exploration of the core ideas around 2-hop questions, we think k-hop questions with k>2 are out of scope for this paper. We focus on 2-hop questions since we believe that they are the most realistic questions that an end user might ask an NLP system. We reviewed datasets that had 3-hop questions, such as Musique, and as we say in the paper, we found them to be very unrealistic and hard even for us to understand. 

We do agree though that 3-hop (and k-hop for k>3) questions are interesting to study from an intellectual and experimental viewpoint, and we did experiment with them a bit (this did not end up in the paper), and found self-ask to successfully answer such questions in our limited experiments. To show you just one 3-hop example, given the 1-shot prompt: 

```
Question: Who is the wife of the U.S. President that served in office when Billie Eilish was born?
Are follow up questions needed here: Yes.
Follow up: When was Billie Eilish born?
Intermediate answer: Billie Eilish was born on December 18, 2001.
Follow up: Who was the U.S. President on December 18, 2001?
Intermediate answer: George W. Bush was the U.S. President on December 18, 2001.
Follow up: Who is the wife of George W. Bush?
Intermediate answer: George W. Bush's wife is Laura Bush.
So the final answer is: Laura Bush.
```

We give the test-time question to GPT-3 (davinci-002):
```
Question: Who is the father of the successor of the person who gave the "I Am Prepared to Die" speech? 
```
And the model correctly answers it:
```
Are follow up questions needed here: Yes. 
Follow up: Who gave the "I Am Prepared to Die" speech? 
Intermediate answer: Nelson Mandela gave the "I Am Prepared to Die" speech. 
Follow up: Who was the successor of Nelson Mandela? 
Intermediate answer: Thabo Mbeki was the successor of Nelson Mandela. 
Follow up: Who is the father of Thabo Mbeki? 
Intermediate answer: Govan Mbeki is the father of Thabo Mbeki. 
So the final answer is: Govan Mbeki.
```
We’ve seen this work with more 3-hop questions and so have reason to believe that self-ask would work with k-hop questions for k>2, but we leave that for future work to thoroughly and empirically explore.

We agree with the reviewer that since our paper only discusses 2-hop questions, we should not use the term ‘multi-hop’ and instead just use the term 2-hop, and will fix that in the next draft. 

In addition, you point to **Qui et al** as containing **more tasks that might be relevant to self-ask**. We pick the first dataset used in Qui et al- COGS, and pick the example shown in Figure 1 of that paper to try self-ask on. And so, using davinci-002 we use the following prompt:
```
Question: What is the expression for "The girl"? 
Are follow up questions needed here: No. 
So the final answer is: girl(x) 

Question: What is the expression for "The cat"? 
Are follow up questions needed here: No. 
So the final answer is: cat(x) 

Question: What is the expression for "The boy"?
Are follow up questions needed here: No. 
So the final answer is: boy(x) 

Question: What is the expression for "The cat loves the girl"? 
Are follow up questions needed here: Yes. 
Follow up: What is the expression for "The cat"? 
Intermediate answer: cat(x) 
Follow up: What is the expression for "The girl"? 
Intermediate answer: girl(x) 
Follow up: What is the expression for "The cat loves the girl"? 
So the final answer is: love(cat(x),girl(x)) 

Question: What is the expression for "The hedgehog sees the cat"? 
Are follow up questions needed here: Yes. 
Follow up: What is the expression for "The hedgehog"? 
Intermediate answer: hedgehog(x) 
Follow up: What is the expression for "The cat"? 
Intermediate answer: cat(x) 
Follow up: What is the expression for "The hedgehog sees the cat"? 
So the final answer is: see(hedgehog(x),cat(x))
```
We then feed the question show at the bottom of Figure 1 in the COGS paper:
```
Question: What is the expression for "The boy loves the hedgehog"?
```

And then the model automatically generates the correct answer:
```
Are follow up questions needed here: Yes. 
Follow up: What is the expression for "The boy"? 
Intermediate answer: boy(x) 
Follow up: What is the expression for "The hedgehog"? 
Intermediate answer: hedgehog(x) 
Follow up: What is the expression for "The boy loves the hedgehog"? 
So the final answer is: love(boy(x),hedgehog(x)) 
```

This is just one example, and we do agree that a further, empirical evaluation of self-ask on this task would be an interesting direction for future work.

content.title: part 2
content.comment:
1. Thank you for pointing out that our paper is clearly written. About your points in the ‘clarity’ section:
Actually the colors in the diagram are different because the data we present is different. In Figure 1,  blue is for when the LM answers the 2-hop question correctly, and green is for when it answers, separately, both 1-hop sub-questions correctly. In Figure 4 green means the same thing, but this time yellow shows the accuracy for self-ask (this doesn’t appear in Figure 1). We will try to clarify this. 
2. *“What is the reason for the self-ask method answering more compositional questions than separate 1-hop questions in Figure 4?"*
That’s a great question! Here’s our hypothesis for why this happens: When we ask a 1-hop question (green) we have a 2-shot prompt. When we use self-ask to answer a 2-hop question (yellow), we have a 1-shot prompt. So it would look something like this (text in <> are our annotations):
```
<prompt 1-shot example> 
Question: Who was President of the United States when Billie Eilish was born?
Are follow up questions needed here: Yes. 
Follow up: When was Billie Eilish born? 
Intermediate Answer: Billie Eilish was born on December 18, 2001. 
Follow up: Who was President of the United States in 2001? 
Intermediate Answer: George W. Bush. 
So the final answer is: George W. Bush

<test time question> 
Question: Who was President of the United States when Matt Damon was born? 
Are follow up questions needed here: Yes. 
Follow up: When was Matt Damon born? 
Intermediate Answer: Matt Damon was born on October 8, 1970. 
Follow up: Who was President of the United States in 1970? 
Intermediate Answer: Richard Nixon was President of the United States in 1970. 
So the final answer is: Richard Nixon
```

Notice that when it came time to answer the final 1-hop subquestion here, there were already 3 answered 1-hop subquestions (2 in the prompt and 1 in the previously-generated part of the answer to the Matt Damon inference-time question). So to answer that final question the model had 3 previous answers to look at, while in the 1-hop case the prompt had just 2 examples. 

So we think that this might make performance with self-ask with just a 1-shot prompt better than the performance of the 2-shot prompt for the 1-hop questions. 

We will clarify this in the next draft. 
  
  
  
 
## Summary

We agree with you that implementing self-ask for k-shot questions, with k>2 would be an interesting and challenging research direction, but we believe that this would be better done by a follow-up paper. We believe the same is true for the semantic parsing tasks shown in Qui et al. 

You point to our other contributions in the compositionality gap and in the self-ask + search engine system, and we hope you agree with us that these contributions will be exciting to the ICLR community.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Big language models have shown impressive abilities to solve NLP problems. It is natural to assume they can solve single-step problems well and decompose multi-step problems into sub-problems. This paper studies the ability of language models to solve multi-step reasoning tasks from correctly composing the answers to sub-problems. It defines a metric called compositionality gap to measure how often models can correctly answer all sub-problems  but not generate the overall solution. It observes that in the GPT-3 family of models, as model size increases, the single-hop question answering performance improves faster than the multi-hop performance does. The compositionality gap does not decrease. The paper interprets the results to mean that big models show no corresponding improvement to perform compositional reasoning. The paper presents an elicitive prompting, e.g. chain of thought, called self-ask to narrow the compositionality gap. Self-ask explicitly asks itself (and then answers) follow-up questions before answering the initial question. The paper also shows that self-ask's structured prompting allows for easy plug in a search engine to answer the follow-up questions, which can further improve accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1. The paper proposes a metric called compositionality gap to measure big language models ability to solve multi-step problems.

2. The paper presents self-ask, an elicitive prompting similar to chain of thought to improve big LMs ability to solve compositional reasoning tasks. 

3. The method is evaluated on four datasets, Compositional Celebrities (CC), Musique, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and a new dataset, Bamboogle (this new dataset is designed by manually creating compositional questions that are simple enough for a popular internet search engine to propose an answer to but hard enough so the answer it proposes is incorrect).

Weaknesses
1. Compared with Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10625), the paper does not seem to have much novelty. Least-to-most prompting essentially decomposes into sub-problems by querying LMs. 

2. Self-ask performs marginally better than chain-of-thought on 2WikiMultiHopQA and Musique. It only performs much better than chain-of-thought on Bamboogle. I wonder least-to-most prompting which improves on chain-of-thought would perform better than self-ask.

3. There are even more principled methods, 
Maieutic Prompting: Logically Consistent Reasoning with Recursive Explanations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11822

4. The paper should evaluate on more reasoning datasets and tasks, e.g. StrategyQA, TimeDial, high school reading comprehension and those in Big-Bench (beyond the Imitation Game benchmark https://arxiv.org/pdf/2206.04615.pdf)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Compositionality gap is a bit confusing. Compositional generalization is well defined for NLP problems. Instead of compositional reasoning, it is more clear to just use multi-step reasoning. Otherwise, the paper is mostly written clearly. 

However, I do not find much novelty when compared with least-to-most prompting and maieutic prompting.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper considers an important problem which is to improve multi-step reasoning with answering intermediate questions. However, the paper is not particularly novel given least-to-most prompting and maieutic prompting. Furthermore, it does not have deep insights on whether self-ask represents genuine improvements across a wide range of reasoning tasks. Evaluation on more datasets will help,

== post authors' response

The comparison results with Least-to-most (LtM) on Musique and 2Wiki are not conclusive. Like LtM, self-ask is very much a heuristic method. Therefore, extensive evaluation results on several datasets are required to have enough empirical evidence. I do not find adding a search engine is a contribution. It introduces more problems that the paper does not address, e.g. search engine often returns whole pages and you have to extract the relevant answers. As a result, I keep my existing rating.

content.title: Novelty compared to Least-to-most and Maieutic Prompting
content.comment:
Thank you for your review! We’re glad you liked our compositionality gap metric, our self-ask prompt and the new dataset we created - Bamboogle. 

You questioned the novelty compared to least-to-most and Maieutic Prompting. The **compositionality gap described in our paper is a new result** that did not appear in previous papers, and shows a major weakness in the strongest publicly accessible LM – GPT-3. While larger variants of GPT-3 understand more about the world, the compositionality gap doesn’t narrow when the parameter count is increased - meaning that larger models are not able to compose the facts they know better than smaller models.
An **additional point of novelty is combining a search engine with an LM in a simple manner, with no finetuning on special data, no training or finetuning with an RL objective, and without even a special syntax**. This is not something that has been done before, and we believe that it is a significant new contribution. 
The structure of our self-ask prompt is what enables this very simple integration with a search engine, which is another benefit of our prompting method. 

In addition, we believe that our prompting method is a substantial improvement over other methods, such as chain of thought and least to most (LtM). We show in the paper that it performs better than chain of thought. As we discuss later in this comment, **Maieutic Prompting is not comparable to self-ask, since it only works for true/false questions**. 

We'll be happy to add a much more detailed comparison of self-ask and these other methods (Maieutic Prompting and LtM) in the next version of the draft. 

## Comparison with Least-to-Most
We believe that our paper presents a novel contribution over LtM for the following reasons:
1. The **least-to-most paper did not show any results on open-domain question answering**, instead focusing on synthetic tasks like letter manipulation and SCAN. Our paper is the first to show that elicitive prompts such as chain of thought and self-ask can do well on open-domain question answering. In our view, the synthetic/algorithmic/symbolic tasks presented in LtM are slightly easier to tackle than open-domain QA, since for open domain QAing a deep world-knowledge is needed and the answer set is the entire vocabulary and not a very limited set of options. 
2. Self-ask requires just 1 API call to answer any question, whereas LtM requires *multiple* API calls, which makes it slower at runtime and harder to implement. For example, to answer a 2-hop question with LtM, you would have to make an initial API call to decompose the question into two subquestions, and then you would have to make another API call for the first subquestion and a final API call for the final subquestion (for a total of 3 API calls). With self-ask, only 1 API call is made to answer that question. While the difference between 1 and 3 API calls may not seem huge, this simplicity makes self-ask much easier to implement and extend - **you don’t even need to write any code to implement self-ask**! You can just copy-paste our prompt and then write your question and feed it to GPT-3 (or any other LM) using a web interface. 
3. LtM did not release any code or even a demonstration of how to use their method. We’ve searched and could not find *any* public project that has reproduced it. LtM is currently [under review at ICLR](https://openreview.net/forum?id=WZH7099tgfM) and its reviewers have also noted that it’s not clear how to reproduce it. In contrast, our self-ask method is reproducible since no code is needed - and we’ve already heard from multiple groups that have successfully reproduced it.

content.title: Novelty compared to Least-to-most and Maieutic Prompting (part 2)
content.comment:
4. Nonetheless, we did our best to reimplement LtM on top of our codebase.  This took approximately 2 hours, because of the complexity of making multiple API calls and the two distinct steps in least to most- decomposition and solving.  For comparison, chain of thought took approximately 5 minutes to implement on top of our codebase because it just required a change of prompt. **The simplicity of self-ask means that it is much more reproducible and understandable than LtM. As our table below shows, the implementation of LtM, as it is described in their paper, leads to substantially worse results than self-ask.** We noticed that in the ‘solve’ step, GPT-3 would solve the first subquestion and then immediately ask another sub-question before stopping. We would then feed the next sub-question from the decompose step, but this would lead to a mismatch between the current input question and the current context. This is an issue that self-ask solves, since in self-ask the solving and subquestion formulation is done at once. 
Still, we fixed this issue by adding a ‘stop’ token to the API call. This was not mentioned in the LtM paper, but we found this to substantially improve performance, and so we are posting those results here as well. Our improved LtM method obtains worse results than self-ask on 2Wiki and comparable results on Musique. Still, as the second table shows, **least-to-most requires outputting many more tokens than self-ask, and so is much slower.** 

5. LtM also requires outputting more tokens than self-ask because in the decompose step it outputs the sub-questions, which then have to be re-stated in the ‘solving’ phase. Self-ask simply outputs a sub-question and then immediately answers it. Empirically (see table below) , on Musique we found that LtM required 53% more tokens than self-ask and on 2WikiMultiHopQA it required 48% more tokens than self-ask. In practice this would mean that using **LtM would be around 50% slower than using self-ask.**



Accuracy (%) of self-ask compared to least-to-most (as described in their paper) and compared to our improvement of least-to-most (not discussed in their paper).
|                                             | Musique | 2Wiki |
|---------------------------------------------|---------|-------|
| Least-to-Most (as described in their paper) | 10.2    | 5.5   |
| Least-to-Most + our modification            | 16.8    | 29.0  |
| Self-ask                                    | 16.3    | 35.5  |


LtM, as described, performs much worse than self-ask. With our modification it performs comparably to self-ask on Musique but still much worse on 2Wiki. 

In all cases, LtM is much slower than self-ask.

This table shows the number of tokens (lower is better) needed on average to generate the solution in each dataset, for each method:

|                                             | Musique | 2Wiki |
|---------------------------------------------|---------|-------|
| Least-to-Most (as described in their paper) | 1064    | 899   |
| Least-to-Most + our modification            | 1020    | 844   |
| Self-ask                                    | 663     | 569   |

For both the original LtM and our improved version of it, self-ask is much faster. 

Note- All numbers here were obtained using davinci-002 (the strongest available version of GPT-3) and the numbers here are unfortunately not directly comparable to the numbers in the paper. We’ve discovered here that davinci-002 is constantly being updated and improved. For example, in our paper, self-ask obtains 13.8 on Musique, and now, using the same code and same data it has obtained 16.3 accuracy.  

Thanks for pointing our attention to LtM, we will clarify these important points in the next version of the paper. 

## Maieutic Prompting
Maieutic Prompting (MP) is a method that is only applicable to true/false questions, and not applicable to open-domain question answering, which is the topic we deal with in this paper.  Their method relies on breaking down a statement that can be true or false into sub-statements that are either true or false. MP can not be used for generating an answer to a question. Thank you for bringing up this work, we will point out this difference in our next draft. 

## Other tasks

We agree with the reviewer that evaluating self-ask on more datasets would be insightful, but were already beyond the page limit and decided to focus in this paper on open-domain questions, which we feel are some of the most challenging benchmarks in NLP right now. This is because these questions require a vast amount of world-knowledge and the answers are not true/false or come from a limited set of options- the answer can be any word or phrase. 
We agree that TIMEDIAL and StrategyQA are interesting datasets, but we would like to point out that TIMEDIAL is a multiple-choice dataset and StrategyQA is a yes/no dataset, and so we believe the datasets we test on are more challenging.

content.comment:
### Clarity 
Thanks for pointing out that our paper is clearly written. We agree that the term ‘compositionality gap’ could be confused with ‘compositional generalization’ and so we dedicated a few sentences to compositional generalization in the related works section, and we will expand on that to make sure there isn’t any confusion. 

## Summary 
We hope we've explained why our paper presents a novel contribution over Least-to-most prompting and Maieutic Prompting. To summarize our rebuttal: maieutic prompting is not applicable to the open domain questions we study here. Least-to-most is about 50% slower than self-ask, and implementing the method as described in the paper leads to much worse results on the open-domain question answering datasets we studied. 

In addition, our paper was the first to show the compositionality gap, and our self-ask + search engine system is the first system that can make search queries from an LM without training or finetuning on special data, without using an RL objective and without even using a special syntax. 

We hope you agree with us that these contributions will be of interest to the ICLR community.

content.title: Your implementation of least-to-most prompting is wrong
content.comment:
"We noticed that in the ‘solve’ step, GPT-3 would solve the first subquestion and then immediately ask another sub-question before stopping." 

This shows that your implementation of least-to-most prompting is not correct. From the least-to-most prompting paper, "**sequentially solves the subproblems, whereby solving a given subproblem is facilitated by the model's answers to previously solved subproblems**". Fig 1 in the paper illustrates how least-to-most prompting solves a math word problem. The paper provided full prompts for all tasks and sampled generated results in the main text and appendix. 

The least-to-most prompting paper has results on SCAN, DROP, and GSM8K. All these are widely used reasoning tasks in the literature to compare the performance of different methods.

In addition, there is another recent paper which has successfully applied least-to-most prompting to solve CFQ ( a really challenging natural language QA task over a knowledge graph) with remarkable results: https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15003

display_title: Details about our implementation of LtM (part 1)

content.title: Details about our implementation of LtM (part 1)
content.comment:
Hi Denny! 

<For context: Denny is the first author of Least-to-most.>


This response includes exact details on how we implement least-to-most and an exact example of the two stages that anyone can try with the online GPT-3 playground. In summary, we tried our best to reproduce least-to-most prompting based on the description in the paper. **You point to an error that we described in our initial response, and as we said in the initial response, we’ve fixed that error in our “LtM with stopping” implementation. Still, that implementation is 50% slower than self-ask, and achieves similar or worse performance on our two datasets.**

Below we show an example of LtM working on a question from the 2Wiki development set, and so we believe our implementation of LtM is correct. 

We believe that the fact that LtM is slower than self-ask is something that is clear just from the paper, without even running any experiments. LtM generates the sub-questions in the first step and then repeats them in the second step, whereas self-ask just asks the sub-questions once. In addition, LtM has two different prompts with lots of overlap, whereas self-ask only uses one prompt. 

To clarify – we do not doubt that least-to-most prompting works – however, since there is no open-source publicly available, this is as close as we can get to re-implementing least-to-most. 

We’re not sure why you linked to a paper that uses LtM for a new set of tasks, but if this was to counter our claim that LtM has not been reproduced- the paper you link to is written by you and 2 other authors who were on LtM. Therefore we do not think that this could be considered a reproduction of your LtM results. 

We would like to reiterate our earlier point that, **self-ask obtains better results overall than LtM, is ~50% faster, and is much easier to implement (no code is necessary- simply copy paste our prompt from the paper).** 

---------------

## Implementing least to most

Least to most has two stages: 

In the first stage we decompose the test-time compositional question into multiple simpler subquestions. So the prompt we use in 2Wiki is:

```
Q: Who lived longer, Theodor Haecker or Harry Vaughan Watkins?
A: To answer the question "How old was Theodor Haecker when he died?", we need to know: "How old was Theodor Haecker when he died?", "How old was Harry Vaughan Watkins when he died?".

Q: Why did the founder of Versus die?
A: To answer the question "Why did the founder of Versus die?", we need to know: "Who founded Versus?", "Why did that person die?"

Q: Who is the grandchild of Dambar Shah?
A: To answer the question "Who is the grandchild of Dambar Shah?", we need to know: "Who is the child of Dambar Shah?", "Who is the child of of that person?".

Q: Are both director of film FAQ: Frequently Asked Questions and director of film The Big Money from the same country?
A: To answer the question "Are both director of film FAQ: Frequently Asked Questions and director of film The Big Money from the same country?", we need to know: "Who directed the film FAQ: Frequently Asked Questions?", "Who directed the film The Big Money?","What is the nationality of the director of the film FAQ: Frequently Asked Questions?","What is the nationality of the director of the film The Big Money?".
```

We then append our test time question:
```
Q: Which company owns the manufacturer of Learjet 60?
```

And then we send that to GPT-3 (davinci-002) and it correctly returns:
```
A: To answer the question "Which company owns the manufacturer of Learjet 60?", we need to know: "Who manufactures Learjet 60?", "Which company owns that manufacturer?".
```

We now need to parse out these 2 subquestions from the returned text and move on to the next step. 

The next step is the ‘solve’ step, where we get the actual answer for the input compositional question.

content.title: Details about our implementation of LtM (part 2)
content.comment:
The ‘solve’ prompt we use for 2Wiki is:

```
Who lived longer, Theodor Haecker or Harry Vaughan Watkins?

Q: How old was Theodor Haecker when he died?
A: Theodor Haecker was 65 years old when he died.

A: Harry Vaughan Watkins was 69 years old when he died. The answer is Harry Vaughan Watkins.

Why did the founder of Versus die?

Q: Who founded Versus?
A: Gianni Versace.
Q: Why did that person die?
A: Gianni Versace was shot and killed on the steps of his Miami Beach mansion on July 15, 1997. The answer is shot.

Who is the grandchild of Dambar Shah?

Q: Who is the child of Dambar Shah?
A: Dambar Shah (? – 1645) was the king of the Gorkha Kingdom. He was the father of Krishna Shah.
Q: Who is the child of that person?
A: Krishna Shah (? – 1661) was the king of the Gorkha Kingdom. He was the father of Rudra Shah. The answer is Rudra Shah.

Are both director of film FAQ: Frequently Asked Questions and director of film The Big Money from the same country?

Q: Who directed the film FAQ: Frequently Asked Questions?
A: Carlos Atanes.
Q: Who directed the film The Big Money?
A: John Paddy Carstairs.
Q: What is the nationality of the director of the film FAQ: Frequently Asked Questions?
A: Carlos Atanes is Spanish.
Q: What is the nationality of the director of the film The Big Money?
A: John Paddy Carstairs is British. The answer is no.
```


We then feed in the input compositional question and the first parsed subquestion: 

```
<insert prompt from above here>
Which company owns the manufacturer of Learjet 60?

Q: Who manufactures Learjet 60?
```

GPT-3 correctly says:

```
A: Bombardier Aerospace.
```

And then we make a 3rd API call- we feed in the second subquestion and get an answer to that question and a final overall answer:

```
<insert prompt from above and answer to first sub-question here>
Q: Who owns Bombardier Aerospace?
A: Bombardier Inc. The answer is Bombardier Inc.
```

And that is correct!

## Bug with davinci-002 when implementing LtM as described in the paper


We know that the behavior we describe in our rebuttal comment is weird, but there is a weird behavior that happens when you use LtM with davinci-002. Here’s an example from 2WikiMultiHopQA:

The compositional question is: 
```
Who is the child of Caroline LeRoy's spouse?
```

We first complete the decompose step of LtM, which correctly returns:
```
<insert decomposition prompt from above>

Q: Who is the child of Caroline LeRoy's spouse?
A: To answer the question "Who is the child of Caroline LeRoy's spouse?", we need to know: "Who is Caroline LeRoy's spouse?", "Who is the child of that person?".
```

(Where everything except the last line is the prompt and the last line is the text generated by davinci-002 given the prompt.)

This means that the two sub-questions that we have to feed in sequentially are: "Who is Caroline LeRoy's spouse?", "Who is the child of that person?".

Now, for the ‘solve’ step (where the error occurs), we use the ‘solve prompt’ with the compositional question at the end and the first sub-question from the ‘decompose’ step:
```
<insert solve prompt from above’

Who is the child of Caroline LeRoy's spouse?

Q: Who is Caroline LeRoy's spouse?
```

And we ask davinci-002 to generate a completion (temperature = 0, top-p = 1, no stop tokens, as in the paper). davinci-002 generates:

```
A: Caroline LeRoy's spouse is Jean-Baptiste Charcot. 
Q: Who is the child of that person? 
A: Jean-Baptiste Charcot (1825 – 1893) was a French explorer and oceanographer. He was the father of Jean-Louis-Ernest Charcot. The answer is Jean-Louis-Ernest Charcot.
```

And that’s the error we described! GPT-3 answers the first subquestion and then **during the solve stage** it makes up its own 2nd subquestion (which happens to be equivalent in this case to the generated 2nd sub-question from the decompose stage, but this isn’t always the case). This might seem weird at first, but this is what happens. You can copy paste this prompt and go to https://beta.openai.com/playground to replicate this. 

Moving on, because LtM method has to feed in the next subquestion, what happens is this:
(remember, the 2nd subquestion from the decompose step was *Who is the child of that person?*)

```
…<beginning of prompt is same as before>...

Who is the child of Caroline LeRoy's spouse? 

Q: Who is Caroline LeRoy's spouse? 
A: Caroline LeRoy's spouse is Jean-Baptiste Charcot. 
Q: Who is the child of that person? 
A: Jean-Baptiste Charcot (1825 – 1893) was a French explorer and oceanographer. He was the father of Jean-Louis-Ernest Charcot. The answer is Jean-Louis-Ernest Charcot. Q: Who is the child of that person? 
A: Jean-Louis-Ernest Charcot (1867 – 1936) was a French neurologist and psychiatrist. He was the father of Jean-Baptiste Charcot. The answer is Jean-Baptiste Charcot.
```

content.comment:
And then the model returns a different answer, because given the context the second question has a different answer now. We observed the original implementation of LtM making this error with davinci-002 many times. 

Anyways, the fix is simple, and the way to do it is to just stop generation at the ‘solve’ step whenever a newline token is generated. This was not described in the LtM paper, but when we applied this it substantially improved results. 

But still, as our rebuttal comment shows, on Musique and 2Wiki, even **LtM with stopping achieves similar or worse performance to self-ask while being ~50% slower.**

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper analyzes whether large language models can answer multi-hop, compositional questions via an automatically constructed dataset, Compositional Celebrities, composed of 2-hop questions. The authors find that although the model gets better with scale at answering compositional questions, this is due to the fact that the model acquires knowledge about their sub-questions, rather than an improved ability of composing knowledge from the sub-questions. To address this fact, the authors propose an elicitive prompting technique, which basically primes the model to decompose the question into the relevant sub-questions. The proposed elicitive prompt technique improves the performance w.r.t to direct prompting and also over chain-of-thought on a novel manually sourced dataset of ~100 questions, Bamboogle.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- *Proposed approach is simple and effective*: I think the most interesting results are: 1) the integration with the search engine; and 2) the fact that self-ask can generalize to Bamboogle while being prompted to solve 2WikiMultiHopQA, and can do so better than Chain-of-Thoughts. 

- *Paper is well-written and clear*: I found the paper very clear and enjoyable to read.

Weaknesses:
- *Experimental setting seems simplistic*: One thing that bugs me a bit is that the experimental setting right now seems simplistic and I am left to wonder whether this method can actually be useful for some settings. I imagine this method being useful in web search, when users can ask complex questions that the search engine can't answer. The authors tried to mimic this setting by manually creating Bamboogle,  which is composed of questions that the search engine can't answer, and on which Self-Ask is shown succeed to some extent. In a more realistic setting, I imagine that the distribution of web queries / questions might be pretty "wild", much more diverse than the kind of questions present in Bamboogle. I appreciated the fact that the improvement on Bamboogle has been obtained by using prompts tuned on 2WikiMultiHopQA (thus putting the model in a situation of distribution shift), but I feel that there is a very small distribution shift between Bamboogle and 2WikiMultiHopQA, both being mined from Wikipedia and mostly composed of 2-hops reasoning. Therefore, first of all, I wonder if the authors could think about coming up with a more convincing setting to show the potential of the approach in a realistic scenario. Some questions that could shed light on the results could be:

1) What happens if the authors try their method for answering realistic web queries contained in Natural Questions ?
3) What is the performance gap when using prompts from a different category on Compositional Celebrities ? Right now the model uses a prompt tailored to each category.

- *Novelty with respect to previous works*: Decomposing a multi-hop question in a series of single-hop questions has received considerable amount of attention in the literature. The proposed method can be seen like an "in-context" formulation of the sub-question decomposition problem. Nevertheless, I think the authors do a good job in acknowledging related works. A reference the authors might also want to include is the following recent work: https://aclanthology.org/2022.coling-1.142.pdf. Due to considerable similarity with these approaches, the authors might consider being a bit more explicit in framing their method with respect to relevant previous work directly in the main text. Moreover, I wonder:

3) How does the method compare to *least-to-most* prompting? Why this baseline is not included in the paper?

- *Baselines for 2WikiMultiHopQA*: I am wondering if it is possible to have some supervised baselines for the datasets tested here, especially for 2WikiMultiHopQA. I think the reference I joined above contains some recent methods one could include for comparison.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Questions and Concerns:

- I am not sure to understand whether in the Self-Ask prompts there are examples where "Are follow-up questions required here:" is sometimes followed by "No"? What happens if you prompt the model with such examples? Can the model solve both compositional and single-hop questions?
- What happens if a similar baseline to least-to-most is used in CC, where the prompt is composed of both the sub-questions and the compositional question?
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper was a pleasure to read. It is clear and self-contained. The Compositional Celebrities dataset, provided it will be released, can benefit the community. Overall, the novelty of the approach consists in performing complex question decomposition with a LM using in-context learning. The integration ability with a search engine is interesting. However, the experimental setting seems a bit simplistic, and therefore I feel that more evidence is needed to understand whether the approach can perform well in a more realistic scenario. I hope the rebuttal phase can elucidate this and my other questions :-)

content.title: Experimental setting and comparison to previous work
content.comment:
Thank you for your review of our paper! We’re happy to see that you liked our self-ask + search engine system and the fact that the standalone self-ask method can do well on Bamboogle even though in the prompt it only sees questions from a different domain (2WikiMultiHopQA).


## Experimental setting
In response to your concern:

> The experiments on 2WikiMultiHopQA and Musique are too simple

It's certainly true that these datasets contain less diversity than NaturalQuestions, but **they require much more challenging reasoning** - and we are the first work to even attempt these datasets few-shot (i.e. without training on thousands of examples). Our self-ask method only requires 4-6 examples in the prompt, and obtains pretty good performance on both datasets. Of course, we don’t approach the supervised baselines, but we do quite well considering the fact that we observed at most 6 examples from the training set. In addition, another important factor is that previous supervised models have also used context paragraphs from Wikipedia to answer these questions. Our results on 2WikiMultiHopQA and Musique are accomplished with *no* context at all- we’re just using the LM. We think these 2 constraints (no context, no training on thousands of examples) make **these datasets particularly challenging for LMs, and we think it’s surprising that our LMs were able to do so well**. 

Here’s a question self-ask answers correctly from the development set of 2WikiMultiHopQA:
```
Question: In what year was the successor of Sperry Corporation established?
```

And here’s how self-ask (using the davinci-002 LM and the 2WikiMultiHopQA prompt from our paper) answers it:

```
Are follow up questions needed here: Yes. 
Follow up: What was the name of the successor company? 
Intermediate Answer: The successor company was Unisys. 
Follow up: When was Unisys established? 
Intermediate Answer: Unisys was established in 1986. 
So the final answer is: 1986
```

We’re impressed that this answer was achieved without any context paragraphs.

> Have you tried using self-ask on NaturalQuestions:

Our paper is centered around the compositionality gap, in which we try to understand if the model would always be able to answer compositional questions for which it knows the answers to the sub-questions of the compositional question. 
As such, we focus on answering 2-hop questions. Although many two hop questions are unrealistic, some of them are realistic. We partially tried to simulate that in Bamboogle, which has some realistic questions, for example “How much protein is there in 4 boiled egg yolks?” or “Can people with celiac eat camel meat?”.
During the project, we did try to evaluate single-hop QA datasets like NaturalQuestions with self-ask, and in our very limited experiments we noticed that self-ask performed about the same as the ‘direct answer’ (vanilla) baseline prompt (simply answering the question right away), sometimes adding more details in the answer. For example, here’s a question from NaturalQuestions that we gave self-ask with the 2WikiMultiHopQA prompt from our paper:
```
How many episodes in season 2 of breaking bad?
```

And here’s the answer from self-ask:
```
Are follow up questions needed here: Yes. 
Follow up: What is the name of the show? 
Intermediate Answer: Breaking Bad 
Follow up: How many seasons are there in total? 
Intermediate Answer: 5 
Follow up: How many episodes are in each season? 
Intermediate Answer: 
Season 1: 7 
Season 2: 13 
Season 3: 13 
Season 4: 13 
Season 5: 16 
So the final answer is: 13
```

Which is correct! For this particular question, the ‘direct answer’ (vanilla) GPT-3 question answering prompt does not return an answer at all. 

We think that this would be an interesting direction for future work to explore, but we think it’s out of scope in this paper, whose primary research question is about compositionality.

content.title: Experimental setting and comparison to previous work (part 2)
content.comment:
> What is the performance gap when using prompts from a different category on Compositional Celebrities ? Right now the model uses a prompt tailored to each category.

You are correct, for compositional celebrities we use a category-specific prompt for each question. If we just use a prompt with questions from a random category for each question, the performance in each category drops by 5% or less. 

We purposefully do our prompting in this category-specific way - for Compositional Celebrities, our goal was not to test the effectiveness of self-ask - we do that with 2Wiki, Musique and Bamboogle. For CC, our goal was to figure out the extent of the compositionality gap. And so we wanted to see what the best performance is that we could get out of the model. And so that’s why we gave it the best prompt for each question. We just wanted to understand how often this interesting phenomenon happened, where the model understands the answer to two sub-questions but can’t combine those pieces of information to answer the compositional question about those two things. Thank you for pointing this out, we will clarify this point in the next draft of the paper. 

> Nevertheless, I think the authors do a good job in acknowledging related works. A reference the authors might also want to include is the following recent work: https://aclanthology.org/2022.coling-1.142.pdf.

Thanks for complimenting our discussion of related work. We were not aware of Wang et al, which came out in the two months before the ICLR submission deadline, but it indeed looks relevant and we will add a reference to it. 

> How does the method compare to least-to-most prompting? Why this baseline is not included in the paper?

1. The **least-to-most paper did not show any results on open-domain question answering**, instead focusing on synthetic tasks like letter manipulation and SCAN. Our paper is the first to show that elicitive prompts such as chain of thought and self-ask can do well on open-domain question answering. In our view, the synthetic/algorithmic/symbolic tasks presented in LtM are slightly easier to tackle than open-domain QA, since for open domain QAing a deep world-knowledge is needed and the answer set is the entire vocabulary and not a very limited set of options.
2. Self-ask requires just 1 API call to answer any question, whereas LtM requires multiple API calls, which makes it slower at runtime and harder to implement. For example, to answer a 2-hop question with LtM, you would have to make an initial API call to decompose the question into two subquestions, and then you would have to make another API call for the first subquestion and a final API call for the final subquestion (for a total of 3 API calls). With self-ask, only 1 API call is made to answer that question. While the difference between 1 and 3 API calls may not seem huge, this simplicity makes self-ask much easier to implement and extend - **you don’t even need to write any code to implement self-ask!** You can just copy-paste our prompt and then write your question and feed it to GPT-3 (or any other LM) using a web interface.
3. LtM did not release any code or even a demonstration of how to use their method. We’ve searched and could not find any public project that has reproduced it. LtM is currently under review at ICLR and its reviewers have also noted that it’s not clear how to reproduce it. In contrast, our self-ask method is reproducible since no code is needed - and we’ve already heard from multiple groups that have successfully reproduced it.
4. Nonetheless, we did our best to reimplement LtM on top of our codebase. This took approximately 2 hours, because of the complexity of making multiple API calls and the two distinct steps in least to most- decomposition and solving. For comparison, chain of thought took approximately 5 minutes to implement on top of our codebase because it just required a change of prompt. **The simplicity of self-ask means that it is much more reproducible and understandable than LtM. As our table below shows, the implementation of LtM, as it is described in their paper, leads to substantially worse results than self-ask.** We noticed that in the ‘solve’ step, GPT-3 would solve the first subquestion and then immediately ask another sub-question before stopping. We would then feed the next sub-question from the decompose step, but this would lead to a mismatch between the current input question and the current context. This is an issue that self-ask solves, since in self-ask the solving and subquestion formulation is done at once. Still, we fixed this issue by adding a ‘stop’ token to the API call. This was not mentioned in the LtM paper, but we found this to substantially improve performance, and so we are posting those results here as well. Our improved LtM method obtains worse results than self-ask on 2Wiki and comparable results on Musique.

replying_to: Replying to Experimental setting and comparison to previous work (part 2)
display_title: Experimental setting and comparison to previous work (part 3)

content.title: Experimental setting and comparison to previous work (part 3)
content.comment:
4. (continued) Still, as the second table shows, **least-to-most requires outputting many more tokens than self-ask, and so is much slower.**
5. LtM also requires outputting more tokens than self-ask because in the decompose step it outputs the sub-questions, which then have to be re-stated in the ‘solving’ phase. Self-ask simply outputs a sub-question and then immediately answers it. Empirically (see table below) , on Musique we found that LtM required 53% more tokens than self-ask and on 2WikiMultiHopQA it required 48% more tokens than self-ask. In practice this would mean that **using LtM would be around 50% slower than using self-ask.**

Accuracy (%) of self-ask compared to least-to-most (as described in their paper) and compared to our improvement of least-to-most (not discussed in their paper).
|                                             | Musique | 2Wiki |
|---------------------------------------------|---------|-------|
| Least-to-Most (as described in their paper) | 10.2    | 5.5   |
| Least-to-Most + our modification            | 16.8    | 29.0  |
| Self-ask                                    | 16.3    | 35.5  |

LtM, as described, performs much worse than self-ask. With our modification it performs comparably to self-ask on Musique but still much worse on 2Wiki. 

In all cases, LtM is much slower than self-ask.

This table shows the number of tokens (lower is better) needed on average to generate the solution in each dataset, for each method:

|                                             | Musique | 2Wiki |
|---------------------------------------------|---------|-------|
| Least-to-Most (as described in their paper) | 1064    | 899   |
| Least-to-Most + our modification            | 1020    | 844   |
| Self-ask                                    | 663     | 569   |

For both the original LtM and our improved version of it, self-ask is much faster. 

Note- All numbers here were obtained using davinci-002 (the strongest available version of GPT-3) and the numbers here are unfortunately not directly comparable to the numbers in the paper. We’ve discovered here that davinci-002 is constantly being updated and improved. For example, in our paper, self-ask obtains 13.8 on Musique, and now, using the same code and same data it has obtained 16.3 accuracy.  

Thanks for pointing our attention to LtM, we will clarify these important points in the next version of the paper. 


> Baselines for 2WikiMultiHopQA: I am wondering if it is possible to have some supervised baselines for the datasets tested here, especially for 2WikiMultiHopQA. 

Thank you for pointing this out! Previous models that have shown results on 2WikiMultiHopQA, have trained supervised models on thousands of examples from the dataset and have used a given context paragraph for each question at test time. We simply use 4 examples in our prompt, do not train on any of the other examples, and do not use any context paragraphs when answering questions. Therefore our results are not comparable to those supervised models that use context. Still, we agree with you that pointing out that our model does not use context paragraphs and was not trained or finetuned on samples from the datasets would be very relevant to our readers, and so we will update our draft to make sure that this is clear. 

## Clarity
> I am not sure to understand whether in the Self-Ask prompts there are examples where "Are follow-up questions required here:" is sometimes followed by "No"? What happens if you prompt the model with such examples? Can the model solve both compositional and single-hop questions?

Since our paper focuses on 2-hop questions, throughout the paper, in all prompts we always say 'Yes' to the 'Are follow-up questions required here?' question. In limited experiments, we found this to not harm the models ability to answer 1-hop questions. As our focus is on 2-hop questions, we don't discuss this in the paper, but will add a clarification about this since we believe some readers might have the same question as you did. 

And yes, we think that for a use case in which a system would have to handle both compositional and 1-hop questions, it would be better to have some questions in the prompt in which the answer to the 'Are follow-up questions required here?' question would be 'No'. In our limited experiments this works well, with the system understanding to ask follow-up questions when given a 2-hop question at inference, and not to ask follow up questions when the test input question is single-hop. 

> What happens if a similar baseline to least-to-most is used in CC, where the prompt is composed of both the sub-questions and the compositional question?

We don't exactly understand your proposed experiments, so if you clarify we might be able to give a better answer, but- self-ask already solves CC. For every compositional question where the model knows the answer to both the subquestions, the model gets the compositional question correct.

content.comment:
(continued) so we don't think that there is any space left to improve results on CC with elicitive prompting.


## Summary
Thanks again for mentioning the clarity of our work, the novelty of our approach to answering compositional questions via prompting, and our new, simple method to integrate a search engine into an LM. We have indeed already released Compositional Celebrities publicly and agree with you that the data will benefit the community.

We hope we’ve convinced you that our work has improved the question answering abilities of LMs even in realistic scenarios. And we hope that you agree with us that our overall list of contributions (Compositionality Gap, Self-ask, Self-ask + search engine, Compositional Celebrities, and Bamboogle) will be exciting to the ICLR community.

content.title: Summary of the discussion
content.comment:
Dear reviewers-

As the discussion period ends soon, we would be grateful to know if our responses answered your questions and concerns.

Here are the main points from the reviews and our rebuttal:

1. Two of the reviewers asked us to compare to least-to-most (LtM) prompting. We ran experiments on Musique and 2WikiMultiHopQA which showed that **LtM is ~50% slower than self-ask and achieves similar or worse performance. In addition, LtM is more complex** to implement and run than self-ask as it requires 3 API calls vs 1 for self-ask, and since it also requires two different prompts versus the single prompt that self-ask requires. 
2. Reviewer **SiwZ asked if self-ask works on 1-hop questions and reviewer p9GT asked if self-ask works on k-hop questions for k>2**. In each response, we showed an **individual example of self-ask working for either** single-hop or 3-hop questions. (Feel free to copy-paste these examples into GPT-3 Playground to play around with these prompts or to reproduce our results there, it's actually really cool to see self-ask automatically solve 3-hop questions). We re-iterated that **our focus in this paper was 2-hop questions, primarily because our paper is framed around the compositionality gap**. This gap, that we are the first to present, shows that GPT-3 commonly knows a pair of facts independently but can't answer a 2-hop question that's made up of these two facts. 
3. The reivewers found our **self-ask prompt to be "simple and effective" and the self-ask + search engine system to an interesting contribution**. In addition, multiple reviewers highlighted the **compositionality gap we discovered** and the **two datasets we created (Bamboogle and Compositional Celebrities)** as contributions that could benefit the community.
4. Two of the reviewers remarked that our paper is well written, with SiwZ writing **"This paper was a pleasure to read. It is clear and self-contained."**



Thank you for your time and effort!

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper studies the ability of language models to solve multi-step reasoning tasks from correctly composing the answers to sub-problems. It proposes a metric to evaluate the capability of language models and proposed a new prompt method to help large language models to solve compositional reasoning tasks. 

The reviewers share similar views on the paper – it is a paper with both strength and weakness. It tries to address an interesting problem, and proposed a reasonable evaluation measure plus a sound solution. On the other hand, its technical novelty is somehow limited, and the empirical performance of the proposed method is not very good either. The authors provided their responses, which have not changed the reviewers’ minds. As a result, I am afraid that we could not accept the paper in its current form.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The technical novelty of the paper is limited (the proposed prompt scheme is similar to prior works), and the empirical results are not very good (only slight increase over baselines).
content.justification_for_why_not_lower_score: It tries to address an interesting problem, and proposed a reasonable evaluation measure plus a sound solution.
